Add end-to-end encrypted private notes to the Switchboard web app in /Users/apple/Desktop/repo-new/switchboard/scaffold/web (React 19 + Vite + TS, no extra libraries: use the browser WebCrypto API only), and write /Users/apple/Desktop/repo-new/switchboard/PROTOCOL.md. Only edit files in scaffold/web/src and that one markdown file. Do not touch scaffold/server, do not run the harness or docker. Existing code to read first: src/components/Thread.tsx, Workspace.tsx, src/api.ts, src/types.ts, src/useSocket.ts, src/styles.css.

Style rules: plain human-looking code, no emoji, no narration comments, short comments only where non-obvious, small files (src/crypto.ts for primitives, src/keyring.ts for key management, src/components/NotesPanel.tsx for UI), reuse the existing api helper and CSS conventions (extend styles.css with a few rules).

Goal: agents leave private notes on a conversation for the other agents in the same workspace. The server must NOT be able to read them.

Scheme (implement exactly this):
- Each user has an ECDH P-256 keypair per workspace, generated in the browser. The private key is stored in IndexedDB as a non-extractable CryptoKey (DB 'switchboard-keys', key by `${sub}:${workspace}`); the public key is exported as SPKI and sent base64 (standard base64, no padding issues: the server accepts [A-Za-z0-9+/_-] plus up to two '=').
- Each workspace has one random AES-GCM 256 key K (the 'workspace key'). K is stored on the server only wrapped: for a recipient, derive a wrap key via ECDH(my private, recipient public) -> HKDF-SHA256 (salt empty, info 'switchboard-wrap-v1') -> AES-GCM 256; encrypt the raw K bytes with a random 12-byte IV; the wrappedKey string is base64(iv || ciphertext). To unwrap, derive the same way using ECDH(my private, wrapper's public key) where the wrapper is `wrappedBy` (a user sub, look up its publicKey from the members list). A user who wraps K for themselves uses their own public key (wrappedBy = own sub).
- A note is AES-GCM encrypted with K, random 12-byte IV, plaintext = UTF-8 text, additionalData = UTF-8 of `${workspace}|${contact}|${author}` so a note cannot be moved to another conversation or attributed to another user. Sent as {ciphertext: base64, iv: base64}.
- Cache the unwrapped K in memory only (module scope), never persist it.

Server API (all under the session cookie, JSON, POSTs/PUTs send content-type application/json; errors are {error:string}):
- PUT /api/keys {workspace, publicKey} -> {ok:true}. Registers my public key for the workspace (replacing it invalidates the key wrapped for the old one, so only call it when no local keypair exists).
- GET /api/workspaces/:ws/keys -> { initialised:boolean, members:[{sub, publicKey, hasKey:boolean}], mine: {wrappedKey, wrappedBy} | null }.
- POST /api/workspaces/:ws/keyring {wrappedKey} -> 201 | 409 (already initialised, or I have not registered a public key). Creates the workspace key: only call when initialised is false; generate K, wrap for myself, post. On 409 reload state.
- PUT /api/workspaces/:ws/keys/:sub {wrappedKey} -> 200 | 403 (I do not hold K) | 409 (target unknown or already has a key). Used to share K with a member who registered a key but has hasKey false. (:sub is a user id like u_ben, encode it.)
- POST /api/conversations/:contact/notes {workspace, ciphertext, iv} -> 201 {id}.
- GET /api/conversations/:contact/notes?workspace=<id> -> {notes:[{id, author, ciphertext, iv, createdAt}]} oldest first. Contact is a phone number like +14155550101: URL-encode in the path.
- WebSocket frame {seq, type:'note.added', contact, note_id, author} arrives on the existing socket (add it to the Frame union in types.ts); on it, if it is for the open conversation, refetch notes.

Behaviour of the notes panel (inside the thread view, e.g. a collapsible 'Private notes' section under the header or beside the messages; label it clearly as encrypted and visible only to the workspace's agents):
1. On open: if no local keypair, generate one and PUT /api/keys. Fetch key state. If I have `mine`, unwrap K and show/decrypt notes. If not and !initialised, create the keyring (generate K). If not and initialised, show 'Waiting for a teammate to share the workspace key' and poll the key state every 5 s.
2. Any member who holds K should, whenever they load key state and see members with hasKey=false, wrap K for each of them and PUT it (silently, do this in keyring.ts as `shareWithPending`; call it from the panel on load and on a 10 s interval while the panel is mounted, and also when the workspace has pending members after the Workspace mounts is NOT required).
3. Decrypt failures (tampered or wrong key) show 'Could not decrypt this note' for that note, not a crash. Show author (resolve to the sub; 'You' for me) and time.
4. Compose box: textarea + 'Add note'; encrypt then POST; show the new note after the notes refetch.
5. If IndexedDB or crypto.subtle is unavailable (non-secure context) show a clear message instead of failing. Note localhost counts as secure.

PROTOCOL.md (for the assessment reviewers; it should be concrete and honest, around 1 to 1.5 pages): who holds which key (user ECDH private key: only in that user's browser, non-extractable IndexedDB; workspace key K: only in browsers, wrapped per member on the server; server holds public keys, wrapped keys, ciphertext, IVs, author id, timestamps, contact id), the exact flows (join, first-member bootstrap, sharing K, writing and reading a note, what the AAD binds), what the server can and cannot do, and exactly THREE attacks the scheme does NOT stop, stated plainly with consequences. Use these three: (1) a malicious or compromised server can substitute a member's public key when K is shared (there is no out-of-band fingerprint verification), then wrap K to itself via a fake member and read all later notes and the existing ones it is given; (2) no forward secrecy or key rotation and no revocation: someone removed from the workspace keeps K and any ciphertext they copied, and a new member who is given K can read all old notes; (3) the server can delete, withhold, or replay notes and cannot be detected (no signature or sequence binding between notes; AAD stops moving across conversations but not dropping or duplicating within one), plus metadata (who wrote, when, how long, which contact) is visible to the server; also mention that XSS in the web app would expose usable keys in the page and that a lost browser profile means lost access. Also state first-write-wins on keys and that an existing holder can be tricked only by the server substituting keys (same as attack 1).

Verify: `cd /Users/apple/Desktop/repo-new/switchboard/scaffold/web && npx tsc --noEmit && npx vite build`, then delete dist/. Also write a small Node script test-free check: add src/crypto.test.ts is NOT needed, but do exercise your crypto.ts primitives once in Node (Node 22 has globalThis.crypto.subtle) with a throwaway script run via `npx tsx` (import crypto.ts, wrap K for a recipient and unwrap, encrypt/decrypt a note, confirm decrypt fails with a wrong AAD), then delete the throwaway script. Keep crypto.ts free of DOM/IndexedDB imports so that works (put IndexedDB code in keyring.ts). Final report (under 250 words): files, anything you assumed, anything unverified.

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in messages from the system in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork runs in the background and keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate. Subagents run in the background; you'll be notified when one completes. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

# Private notes: encryption protocol

Private notes are end-to-end encrypted in the browser with WebCrypto only. The server stores and relays opaque bytes and cannot read note text.

## Who holds what

| Secret / data | Held by | Where |
|---|---|---|
| User ECDH P-256 private key (one per user per workspace) | that user's browser only | IndexedDB `switchboard-keys`, key `${sub}:${workspace}`, non-extractable CryptoKey |
| Workspace key K (random AES-GCM 256) | members' browsers only | memory while the page is open; never persisted in the clear |
| Public keys (SPKI, base64) | server | registered via `PUT /api/keys` |
| Wrapped K, one per member | server | `wrappedKey` + `wrappedBy` |
| Note ciphertext, IV, author id, timestamp, contact id | server | notes table |

The server never sees a private key, K, or note plaintext.

## Flows

**Join.** On first opening the notes panel, the browser generates an ECDH keypair, stores the private key, and registers the public key (`PUT /api/keys`). Registration happens only when no local keypair exists, because replacing a key invalidates the K that was wrapped for the old one. The first registration for a user/workspace wins.

**First-member bootstrap.** If the workspace is not initialised and I have no wrapped key, I generate K, wrap it for my own public key (wrappedBy = me) and `POST .../keyring`. A 409 means someone else got there first; I reload state.

**Sharing K.** Any member holding K, on panel load and every 10 s, looks for members with `hasKey = false` and `PUT`s a wrapped K for each. Wrapping: `ECDH(my private, recipient public)` -> HKDF-SHA256 (empty salt, info `switchboard-wrap-v1`) -> AES-GCM 256 key; encrypt raw K with a random 12-byte IV; `wrappedKey = base64(iv || ciphertext)`. A member without K shows "Waiting for a teammate to share the workspace key" and polls every 5 s. To unwrap, the recipient derives the same key from `ECDH(my private, wrappedBy's public)`, with the wrapper's public key taken from the members list the server returns.

**Writing a note.** AES-GCM with K, random 12-byte IV, plaintext UTF-8, additional data `${workspace}|${contact}|${author}`. Sent as `{ciphertext, iv}`.

**Reading.** Fetch notes, decrypt each with K using AAD built from the workspace, the contact being viewed, and the note's author id as reported by the server. Failure (tampering, wrong key, moved note, changed author) shows "Could not decrypt this note" for that note. The AAD stops a note being moved to another conversation or workspace and stops it being attributed to a different user. Live updates arrive as `note.added` frames, which trigger a refetch.

## What the server can and cannot do

Cannot: read notes, recover K, forge a note that decrypts (it lacks K), edit a note undetected, or move a note to another conversation or author undetected.

Can: see all metadata, delete or withhold notes, replay or duplicate notes, refuse to serve keys, and substitute public keys (see attack 1).

## Attacks this scheme does NOT stop

1. **Public key substitution by the server.** Public keys are trusted as the server reports them; there is no out-of-band fingerprint or safety-number check. A malicious or compromised server can register a fake member with a key it controls, or replace a pending member's public key. A holder of K then wraps K for that key, and the server unwraps it and reads all notes from then on plus every existing note it holds. Because keys are first-write-wins, a real member who registers after the server has planted a key for them is locked out rather than detected. An existing holder is only ever fooled this way: by the server handing over a substituted key.

2. **No forward secrecy, rotation or revocation.** K never changes. Someone removed from the workspace keeps K and any ciphertext they copied, and can read everything written under K, including future notes if they can still obtain ciphertext. A new member given K reads all old notes. A leaked device key or K compromises all notes, past and future.

3. **Dropping, withholding and replaying notes, and metadata.** Notes carry no signature and no sequence binding. The AAD prevents moving a note across conversations or authors but not deleting a note, hiding it from some readers, or duplicating a valid note within the same conversation; none of this is detectable. The server also sees who wrote each note, when, its length, and which contact it concerns.

Also out of scope: XSS in the web app can use the keys in the page (the private key is non-extractable, but the page can still ask the browser to use it, and K is in memory); and losing the browser profile (IndexedDB cleared, new device) loses the private key. Access is only regained if the user re-registers, which in this design requires a new key and a fresh share of K from a teammate, and the server-side state for the old key needs to be reset.
